routes.label: Connect the centers of tangent circles

question:
Four congruent semicircles are inscribed in a square of side length \(1\) so that their diameters are on the sides of the square, one endpoint of each diameter is at a vertex of the square, and adjacent semicircles are tangent to each other. A small circle centered at the center of the square is tangent to each of the four semicircles, as shown below.

[Figure 1](figures/2025_AMC_10B_Q20_question_fig1.svg)

The diameter of the small circle can be written as \((\sqrt{a} + b)(\sqrt{c} + d),\) where \(a,\) \(b,\) \(c,\) and \(d\) are integers. What is \(a + b + c + d?\)
solution:
Connecting circle centers turns tangency into a length relation: externally tangent circles have center distance equal to the sum of their radii.

[Figure 1](figures/2025_AMC_10B_Q20_question_fig1.svg)

Label the square \(ABCD\) counterclockwise starting at the lower-left corner. Let \(R>0\) be the common semicircle radius, and let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the centers of the semicircles on \(AB\) and \(BC\). In the displayed arrangement,
\[
AP=BQ=R,\qquad PB=1-R.
\]
The two semicircles are externally tangent, so \(PQ=2R\). Triangle \(PBQ\) is right at \(B\). Since its hypotenuse and one leg are already multiples of \(R\), the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
PB=\sqrt{(2R)^2-R^2}=\sqrt3\,R.
\]
Now use the full side \(AB\):
\[
1=AP+PB=(1+\sqrt3)R.
\]
Consequently,
\[
2R=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt3}=\sqrt3-1.
\]
This gives \(0<R<1/2\), as required for the semicircle's diameter to fit on a side.

Let \(O\) be the square's center. A quarter-turn about \(O\) carries each semicircle center to the next, so the four centers form a square centered at \(O\). Its side is \(2R\), and its diagonal is \(2\sqrt2\,R\). Hence
\[
OP=\sqrt2\,R.
\]
If \(r>0\) is the small circle's radius, its external tangency to the semicircle centered at \(P\) gives \(OP=R+r\). Therefore
\[
r=(\sqrt2-1)R,
\qquad
2r=(\sqrt3-1)(\sqrt2-1).
\]
We may take \(a=3\), \(b=-1\), \(c=2\), and \(d=-1\). Thus
\[
a+b+c+d=3-1+2-1=3,
\]
so the answer is \(3\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
